lessons.title: Open loop, closed loop, and return ratio
lessons.physicalIntuition: Loop gain describes how a perturbation returns around a specified feedback path. Closing the loop changes disturbance rejection and command response, but only if signs and operating point are preserved.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Derive closed-loop sensitivity and complementary sensitivity from the declared negative-feedback diagram. Define crossover and margins at identified crossings, noting multiple-crossing and phase-convention caveats.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Plots must name the loop, cut/injection point, return-ratio sign, crossing, and operating point. A node ratio is not automatically loop gain.
lessons.interaction: Loop-path highlighting and margin cursor lab
lessons.transferQuestion: If the magnitude crosses unity three times, which phase margin should be reported and what additional evidence is needed?

lessons.title: Damping, peaking, and time response
lessons.physicalIntuition: A stable loop can still ring badly. Phase margin is a local loop-shape clue, while zeros, gain slope, saturation, and large-signal current slew shape the actual transient.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Relate a canonical second-order damping ratio to peaking and step response only under that canonical form, then show why additional poles/zeros break a one-number mapping.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The tuning lab exposes complete loop, closed-loop, and output-impedance frequency responses. A load-step cross-check remains a separate nonlinear validation task because this lab does not synthesize one from phase margin.
assumptions: second-order mappings are approximations outside canonical systems
lessons.interaction: Classify damping and predicted step-response tendencies from the displayed loop shape, then write the separate switched load-step validation you would run
lessons.transferQuestion: Give two loops with similar phase margin but different transient peaking and identify the extra feature responsible.

lessons.title: Phase and bandwidth disambiguation
lessons.physicalIntuition: The same words describe hardware branches, geometric timing, complex angle, and response speed. Ambiguity is a technical error because each quantity predicts different behavior.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Define phase offset as time displacement normalized by period, Bode phase as arg G(jw), phase margin from loop angle at a selected unity crossing, and each bandwidth from a named loop/closed response. Under ideal uniform N-phase timing, summed ripple periodicity can be Nfs, but variable-frequency phases break that shortcut.
lessons.modelingConsequence: UI labels never say only 'phase' or 'bandwidth.' Every metric includes its object and units; per-phase switching-frequency distributions are separated from effective summed ripple.
assumptions: ideal Nfs relation requires equal frequency, symmetry, and spacing
lessons.transferQuestion: Repair this statement: 'The four-phase buck phase is 60 degrees at a 100-kHz bandwidth.'

lessons.title: Crossover versus switching rate
lessons.physicalIntuition: A loop cannot ignore the pulse-generation delay and sampled decisions when its dynamics approach those time scales. A fixed fraction of fs is only a starting screen.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Model delay as exp(-sTd) to expose frequency-dependent phase lag, and compare averaged predictions with sampled-data limits near half switching frequency. No single ratio includes delay, plant order, ripple, or architecture.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The lab may display heuristic zones but cannot score one universal crossover ratio. Switched verification is mandatory for aggressive targets.
lessons.transferQuestion: Why might fs/10 be conservative in one converter and unsafe in another?
